_nota: Banco de preguntas escrito por Claude para el diagnóstico. Los niveles CEFR son una estimación razonada, no una certificación oficial (ver PROMPT_BASE.md: 'sé honesto, es una estimación'). Contenido original, verificado gramaticalmente con confianza alta. Las preguntas con id que empieza en 'lec-a2-3'/'esc-a2-3'/'voc-a2-3' en adelante (y equivalentes en otros niveles) son nuevas del Paso C, marcadas 'revisar: true'. Nota aparte: en todas las preguntas ORIGINALES (de la noche anterior) la respuesta correcta es siempre la opción en el índice 0 -- es un patrón real de los datos que no corregí (cambiarlo requeriría mezclar las opciones al renderizar, un cambio de lógica fuera de este paso); lo marco aquí para que se revise, y en las preguntas NUEVAS sí varié a propósito en qué posición queda la respuesta correcta.

preguntas.texto: Artificial intelligence systems are often trained on large datasets, but the quality of those datasets matters as much as their size. A model trained on biased or incomplete data can produce results that look confident but are actually misleading, which is why data curation has become a central part of responsible AI development.

preguntas.texto: Many engineering teams have adopted code review as a standard practice, not only to catch bugs but also to spread knowledge about the codebase among team members. A thorough review can take time, but teams that skip it often pay for it later with harder-to-fix problems.

preguntas.texto: The notion that technical debt is inherently harmful oversimplifies a more nuanced reality: some debt is taken on deliberately, as a reasonable trade-off to ship a feature quickly, with the understanding that it will be addressed once priorities allow. Problems arise less from the existence of debt itself than from a team's failure to track and eventually repay it.
preguntas.pregunta: What does the passage suggest is the real source of problems with technical debt?
opciones: Failing to track and repay debt that was taken on deliberately
The mere existence of any technical debt at all
Shipping features too quickly in general
Teams that never take on any debt

preguntas.texto: Teams spread across different time zones often rely on asynchronous communication: detailed written updates instead of live meetings. This requires writing more clearly than a quick chat message would, since there's no chance to immediately clarify a misunderstanding, but it also means people can respond when it actually suits their schedule.

Because teams in the same time zone write poorly

preguntas.texto: Estimating how long a software project will take is notoriously difficult, partly because unexpected problems tend to appear only once work has already started. Experienced teams don't try to eliminate this uncertainty; instead, they build in extra time and communicate estimates as ranges rather than exact dates.
preguntas.pregunta: How do experienced teams deal with the uncertainty in estimates, according to the text?
opciones: They eliminate uncertainty completely before starting
They build in extra time and give estimates as ranges
They refuse to give any estimate at all
They only estimate projects that have no unexpected problems

preguntas.texto: The old engineering mantra of moving fast and breaking things assumes that the cost of mistakes stays low enough to be worth the speed gained. That assumption tends to hold for a young product with few users, but it erodes as a system matures and the blast radius of a careless change grows, which is why many teams quietly slow down as they scale, without ever renouncing the idea in public.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the passage, why might a maturing team slow down even without admitting it?
opciones: The cost of mistakes grows as the system's blast radius increases
They have fully renounced the idea of moving fast in public
Young products always have more users than mature ones
Speed stops being valuable to any team at any stage

preguntas.texto: Maintainers of widely used open-source projects often describe a quiet asymmetry: thousands of people benefit from their work, yet only a handful ever contribute back, whether in code, documentation, or even acknowledgment. Burnout, in this telling, has less to do with the coding itself than with the accumulated weight of unpaid, invisible obligation.
preguntas.pregunta: What does the passage suggest is the real source of maintainer burnout?
opciones: The accumulated weight of unpaid, invisible obligation
The coding work itself, regardless of recognition
Having too many contributors helping with the project
A lack of users willing to try the project
